A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that the combination of first-line drugs and second-line drugs can be used to treat MDR-TB.

we found that treatment success for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) was high, but that the treatment success rate was lower for patients infected with extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) and those with MDR-TB who were resistant to at least one fluoroquinolone and/or one of the injectable second-line drugs (category 2).

we have found that the use of second-line drugs in the treatment of multidrug-resistant (MDR) tuberculosis is associated with a higher risk of treatment failure, but the risk is reduced if first-line drug susceptibility testing (DST) is performed before the initiation of second-line drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can now say with a high degree of confidence that patients with extensively drug-resistant (XDR) tuberculosis are more likely to die than those with multidrug-resistant (MDR) tuberculosis.
we need to improve our ability to diagnose TB in children and adolescents, particularly those with HIV.
the current treatment guidelines for MDR-TB, as recommended by the World Health Organization, are not effective.
